ca_hwy_44_boulders.blurb: A small cluster of boulders along Highway 44 in the Lassen area of northeastern California, at roughly 5,000 feet. There are eight problems, running from V1 up to V6, with most falling between V2 and V5. Boulders start to show up a few miles past the town of Viola when driving east from Redding. The problems were climbed years ago, left alone, and picked up again by later visitors, so the list is short and there is room for new lines. It suits a brief stop for bouldering rather than a full day, and other roadside crags and boulder fields sit along the same stretch of highway.

ca_saigon_boulder.blurb: Saigon Boulder is a tall, isolated block high on the hillside in the Buttermilks near Bishop, at about 6,400 feet. It is the topmost boulder on the slope, reached by walking uphill from the roadside parking. The eight problems span V0 to V11: two V0s and a handful of mid-grade lines, with a few hard ones at the top end. One face holds several highball warm-ups, an arete carries the area's best-known line, and another face has a very hard problem. The tall faces make the descent serious, and a beginner may find downclimbing frightening, so plan how you will get down before you start up.

ca_y_crack_area_the.blurb: The Y Crack Area is the first cluster of climbs met on the trail at Dixon Lake in north Escondido, San Diego County, at about 1,100 feet. The formation comes into view as soon as the trail leaves the road, and the walk to its base takes only a couple of minutes. Of the eight routes, six are trad, one is a top rope and one is sport-style. Grades run from 5.3 to 5.11, and most sit between 5.6 and 5.9, which makes it a reasonable place for novice and intermediate climbers. The namesake is an offwidth crack splitting the middle of the face, with a bolted line just to its left.

ca_turtle_rock_south_face.blurb: This is the southern end of Turtle Rock in the Hidden Valley area of Joshua Tree National Park, at roughly 4,200 feet. The routes line a sheltered corridor where the wall is generally overhanging and the quality of the stone varies from good to poor. Eight routes split evenly between sport and trad: the trad lines run from 5.9 to 5.11, while the sport routes are hard, from 5.12 into the 5.14 range. Expect steep, demanding climbing rather than a beginner outing. To reach the base, go around the right-hand end of the formation, passing the Pillars of Pain, turn left and thread through the boulders to the foot of the face.
ca_turtle_rock_south_face.approach: Go around the right-hand end of the formation, passing the Pillars of Pain, then turn left and thread through the boulders to the foot of the south face.

ca_tin_can_alley.blurb: Tin Can Alley is a small, steep canyon of boulders in Holcomb Valley, in the San Bernardino Mountains near Big Bear Lake, at roughly 7,500 feet. It has eight problems, nearly all at the easy end: one at VB, five at V0, and one each at V1 and V2. The problems are tall, and the holds are covered in patina. It is one pocket within a wider group of moderate boulders on the east side of the valley, where the landings are flat and a climber trail runs past almost every problem.

ca_yaks_wall.blurb: Yaks Wall holds the climbs north of the Yaks formations on the East Side of Pinnacles National Park, past the ridge east of the Bear Gulch area, at about 2,000 feet. It has eight routes, six trad and two sport, all between 5.8 and 5.10, with most at 5.10. The climbing leans toward water chutes, wide cracks and chimneys rather than the typical bolted Pinnacles faces. The rock can be loose, and on lightly traveled lines protection may be 15 to 20 feet apart. Some of the routes are multi-pitch.
